text: More than 2,400 years ago, in north-east India, a prince named Mahavira gave up his home to fast and meditate.
Jains believe he was the last of twenty-four great teachers, called Tirthankaras.
src: Magadha, north-east India, 6th or 5th century BCE / Mahavira himself, whose personal name was Vardhamana, was a prince of the Jnatrika clan / At about thirty Mahavira renounced his home and practised severe austerities for some twelve years, fasting, meditating
According to Jain tradition, twenty-four Tirthankaras have appeared in the present age of the world, beginning with Rishabhanatha, an immeasurably distant figure, and ending with Mahavira

text: Jains believe that every living being, from people and animals to plants and insects, has a soul.
So they try never to harm any living thing, and they eat no meat.
src: Every living being, from humans and animals to plants, insects and the tiniest beings in earth, water, fire and air, has a soul
Its ethics rest on ahimsa, non-violence toward all living beings / Jains are strict vegetarians

text: Monks and nuns own nothing and travel on foot, and some sweep the ground before them so as not to crush insects.
Jain merchants built splendid temples, and the hill of Shatrunjaya is crowned with hundreds of shrines.
src: Monks and nuns renounce all possessions, live by the five great vows, travel on foot from place to place / monks and nuns may sweep the ground before them to avoid crushing insects
Merchant communities built splendid temples there / the hill of Shatrunjaya at Palitana is crowned with hundreds of shrines

text: Jain monks were also scholars, writing about grammar, poetry, the stars and mathematics.
The monk Hemachandra guided a king of Gujarat, who forbade the killing of animals in his kingdom.
src: Jain monks were also prolific scholars in many fields. They wrote on logic and philosophy, grammar, poetry, astronomy and mathematics
The Chaulukya king Kumarapala, guided by Hemachandra, promoted Jain ethics in the 12th century, forbidding the slaughter of animals in his realm

text: More than 1,000 years ago, a giant statue of Bahubali, about 17 metres high, was carved from one block of granite.
Every twelve years it is bathed with milk, saffron and flowers.
src: The colossal statue of Bahubali at Shravanabelagola in Karnataka, carved from a single block of granite around 983, stands about 17 metres high
is anointed with milk, saffron and flowers every twelve years

text: The Jain idea of non-violence helped inspire Mahatma Gandhi, who grew up among Jain neighbours.
Today about 4.5 million people in India are Jains, and smaller communities live in other countries.
src: through Mohandas Gandhi, who grew up in Gujarat among Jain neighbours / it helped inspire the non-violent resistance
Today about 4.5 million Indians are Jains, according to the census of 2011, with smaller communities abroad
